## Where the last session left off

- A thousand people on a grid, contacts drawn from the twenty-four neighbours
  within two cells.
- Everyone behaves the same way from the first day to the last.
- Widening the neighbourhood from eight people to twenty-four changed a single
  introduction from one that stayed under 100 infections in 96% of 200 runs to
  one that grew large in 44.5% of them.

This session adds one thing: people who notice what is happening around them.

::: {.notes}
Recap only as far as is needed to start.  The grid, the two-phase update and
`nearby_agents` all carry over unchanged, so nothing about the API is new today.

The last bullet is the hook.  The previous session showed that *who you meet*
changes the epidemic; this one asks what happens when *what you know* changes
too.
:::

## One rule about behaviour

A susceptible person who can see at least $m$ infectious people within
`info_radius` cells takes precautions for that step:

$$
\beta \longrightarrow \beta(1-\alpha).
$$

Three numbers, each of them a modelling assumption:

- `info_radius`, how far a person's information reaches;
- $m$, how many cases it takes before they act;
- $\alpha$, how much good the precautions do.

::: {.notes}
The information radius and the contact radius are separate numbers: one decides
who you can see, the other who can infect you.  Last session had only the second.

Do not sell the wider radius as advance warning, because at $m=1$ it does
nothing.  Contacts come from radius 2, so anybody made aware only by the outer
ring has no infectious contact that step, and awareness is recomputed from
scratch every step, so it carries nothing forward.  The worksheet runs the two
radii in lockstep and every agent holds the same status at every step, in all
eight seeds; only the aware person-day count differs, 4,533 against 2,524 for the
same 47.1 infections.  It starts to matter at $m\ge2$, where a case outside the
contact neighbourhood can help cross the threshold.

That is worth saying rather than hiding, because it also tells the room which way
the Part C comparison leans: the local rule is charged for precautions that could
not have mattered, so the comparison runs against it.

Nothing here makes precautions persist.  Somebody who sees no infection this step
behaves normally again, which is worth flagging before anyone asks.
:::

## The same behaviour, three kinds of information

| Setting | What a person can see |
|---|---|
| `:none` | nothing; last session's model |
| `:local` | the infectious people within `info_radius` cells |
| `:national` | population prevalence $I/N$, observed perfectly and without delay, acting once it passes $\theta$ |

The precautions are identical in all three. Only the trigger differs.

::: {.notes}
This table is the design of the whole session.  Holding efficacy fixed and varying
only the trigger lets the comparison be about targeting, under approximately
matched participation, rather than about how strong an intervention is.  It does
not isolate a single effect: the two rules still differ in who is enrolled and
for how long, and the matching on aware person-days is approximate.

`:national` is the version a compartmental model can already express, as a
transmission rate that falls with prevalence.  Say that now; Part C returns to it.
:::

## Counting how much precaution is taken

Either rule can be made stronger by having more people take precautions for
longer, so comparing outcomes alone proves nothing.

**Aware person-days**: susceptible people taking precautions, times the length
of the step, added up over the epidemic. It measures *participation* in
precautions. It is not a cost, because it says nothing about what a person-day
of precaution is worth giving up.

```julia
function model_step!(model)          # count first, before the commit
    model.aware_days += model.Δt *
        count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model))
    for p in allagents(model); p.status = p.next_status; end
    model.prevalence = infected_count(model) / N
end
```

Match the two rules on that, then compare the epidemics.

::: {.notes}
This is the idea participants are most likely to skip past, so it is worth
stating twice: without a measure of how much precaution was taken, "the local
rule works better" only means "this setting of the local rule was stronger than
that setting of the national one".

Be precise about what it is, because it is easy to slip into calling it a cost.
Every person-day counts the same whether it is a mask or a closed shop, so it is
a proxy for participation and nothing more; turning it into a cost would need
prices this model does not have.  That limitation is one of the discussion
questions.
:::

## The result

```{julia}
#| label: code-slide-ch06b-result
#| echo: false
using Agents, Distributions, Random, StableRNGs, Statistics

const N = 1000
@agent struct Person(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end
infected_count(m) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(m))
recovered_count(m) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(m))

function is_aware(person, model)
    model.information == :none && return false
    model.information == :national && return model.prevalence >= model.θ
    return count(a -> a.status == :I,
                 nearby_agents(person, model, model.info_radius)) >= model.m
end

function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        transmission = is_aware(person, model) ? model.β * (1 - model.α) : model.β
        neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius))
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < transmission
                person.next_status = :I; break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
        person.next_status = :R
    end
end

function model_step!(model)
    model.aware_days += model.Δt *
        count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model))
    for p in allagents(model); p.status = p.next_status; end
    model.prevalence = infected_count(model) / N
end

function run_one(seed; information = :none, α = 0.5, m = 1, θ = 0.05)
    model = StandardABM(Person,
        GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic=true, metric=:chebyshev);
        agent_step!, model_step!,
        properties = Dict(:β=>0.05, :c=>10.0, :γ=>0.25, :Δt=>0.1, :radius=>2,
            :information=>information, :α=>α, :m=>m, :info_radius=>3, :θ=>θ,
            :prevalence=>0.01, :aware_days=>0.0),
        rng = StableRNG(seed))
    for pos in positions(model); add_agent!(pos, model; status=:S, next_status=:S); end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:10]
        model[id].status = :I; model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    steps = 0
    while infected_count(model) > 0
        steps == 10_000 && error("still infectious after 10,000 steps")
        step!(model, 1)
        steps += 1
    end
    return (final = recovered_count(model), aware = model.aware_days)
end

summarise(; kw...) = begin
    runs = [run_one(s; kw...) for s in 7000 .+ (1:8)]
    (final = round(mean(r.final for r in runs); digits = 1),
     aware_days = round(Int, mean(r.aware for r in runs)))
end

(nobody_reacts = summarise(information = :none),
 local_information = summarise(information = :local, m = 1),
 national_information = summarise(information = :national, θ = 0.05))
```

Same precautions. Nearly the same amount of precaution taken. Very different
epidemics.

::: {.notes}
Eight seeds, the same set the worksheet uses, so the numbers on this slide are
the ones participants will reproduce.

Do not explain the mechanism yet.  Put the three rows on the screen, ask the room
why two of them differ so much when the precautions are identical, and let the
worksheet be where they find out.  A large part of the answer is targeting: local
information places its precautions on people whose own neighbourhood holds a
case, and on this grid every transmission happens between neighbours.  Say "a
large part" rather than "the answer": the later assumptions slide explains what
else is built into the comparison.
:::

## Why this needs agents

- The national rule is a function of $I/N$. A compartmental model can carry it
  as $\beta(I)$ and needs no individuals.
- The local rule is a function of *one person's own neighbourhood*.
- Writing it in $S$, $I$ and $R$ would need the number of
  susceptible-infectious neighbour pairs, then triples, and so on. The system
  does not close.

A model whose state is $S$, $I$ and $R$ totals cannot express this rule at all.
An ABM keeps the local configuration directly; network-state, pairwise and
message-passing formulations are other routes to it, usually at the price of a
structural restriction or a closure approximation.

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that justifies the session existing, and it is the one to
protect if time runs short.

Be careful not to oversell.  "Only an ABM can do this" is false: pairwise and
message-passing methods are used for exactly this class of rule, and on some
network structures they are exact.  The honest statement is the one on the slide,
that $S$, $I$, $R$ totals are not enough, and that practical lower-dimensional
routes buy tractability with either a restriction on the contact structure or a
closure whose error is influenced by the neglected higher-order correlations,
which are the same correlations local awareness depends on.
:::

## What the model assumes, and does not {.smaller}

- Anyone close enough to infect you is close enough for you to see: the
  information radius of 3 contains the contact radius of 2. At $m=1$ no
  susceptible person with a current infectious contact-neighbour is missed. That
  containment is a central mechanism built into the comparison, not an
  incidental parameter choice.
- People know their neighbours' status at once and for free. In reality
  infection precedes symptoms and reporting takes days, so protection would
  arrive late.
- Every aware person-day is counted the same, whether it is a mask or a closed
  shop.
- Nobody stays careful once their neighbourhood looks clear.

The measured advantage of local information is an optimistic benchmark, not a
forecast.

::: {.notes}
The first bullet is the mechanism rather than a caveat, so do not hurry it.
Under the Chebyshev metric a ball of radius 3 contains one of radius 2, so any
infectious person who could reach you is inside your information radius, and at
$m=1$ the rule never misses a susceptible person who has a current infectious
contact-neighbour.  It stops holding at $m\ge2$, where
you can have one infectious neighbour and still not act, and the worksheet sweep
prices that: 47 infections at $m=1$ against 140 at $m=2$.

Say that this was built into the comparison rather than discovered by it.  How
much of the local rule's advantage it accounts for has not been decomposed here;
separating containment from targeting would need a run with the information
radius set below the contact radius, which is a good thing to suggest to anyone
asking what to try next.

Both information failures in the second bullet push the same way, which is why
the result should be read as an optimistic benchmark: it is what local
information could achieve if it were free, immediate and perfectly accurate.

The last bullet is the most inviting thing to change, and a good answer to "what
should I try next".  Making precautions persist needs somewhere to keep the
memory, though: a per-agent countdown field set when a case is seen and
decremented each step, which means touching the agent struct, the initialiser and
both stepping functions.  Small, but not a two-line edit.
:::

## Takeaways

- A space defines a neighbourhood; a neighbourhood defines who you meet and
  what you can see, and those need not be the same set.
- Compare behavioural rules at matched participation, or you are comparing
  strengths.
- In these eight seeded runs, a response too weak to break transmission was
  sustained for far longer and averted far less.

::: {.notes}
The mechanism behind it is not specific to this model: precaution is taken per person
per unit time, so how long the epidemic runs is part of how much precaution gets
taken, and a response that merely slows transmission keeps a population careful
for longer than one that stops it.  Whether it holds elsewhere depends on the contact
structure and on how strong "too weak" turns out to be.
:::
